<a id="CA-2-formal-identities-specialise-on-a-disc"></a>

#### CA.2.30 Formal identities specialise on a disc of holomorphy

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/formal-identities-specialise-on-a-disc` · theorem

Let r > 0 and let g, h be complex differentiable on the disc |z| < r, with g(z) ≠ 0 there. If F ∈ ℂ⟦X⟧ satisfies F·T(g) = T(h) in ℂ⟦X⟧ (T the Taylor series at 0), then for every z with |z| < r the series ∑ Fₙ zⁿ converges to h(z)/g(z).

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- g has no zero on the open disc; the radius r is the conclusion's radius of convergence (it may be smaller than the true one).
- No assumption that F converges anywhere: convergence is part of the conclusion.

**Checks.**

- With g = 1 − z, h = 1, F = ∑ Xⁿ: ∑ zⁿ = 1/(1 − z) for |z| < 1.
- The hypothesis g ≠ 0 on the disc cannot be dropped: F = ∑ Xⁿ satisfies F·T(1 − z) = 1 but ∑ zⁿ diverges at |z| = 1 where g vanishes.

**Proof sketch.**

1. h/g is complex differentiable on the disc (quotient rule, g ≠ 0), hence analytic there (`DifferentiableOn.analyticAt`).
2. T(h/g)·T(g) = T(h) by multiplicativity of T (taylor-series-of-a-complex-function); T(g) has constant coefficient g(0) ≠ 0, so it is a unit (`PowerSeries.isUnit_iff_constantCoeff`) and F = T(h/g).
3. Conclude by convergence of the Taylor series of h/g on the disc (`Complex.hasSum_taylorSeries_on_ball`).

**Needs:** [CA.2/taylor-series-of-a-complex-function](#CA-2-taylor-series-of-a-complex-function), `mathlib:Complex.hasSum_taylorSeries_on_ball`, `mathlib:DifferentiableOn.analyticAt`, `mathlib:PowerSeries.isUnit_iff_constantCoeff`, `mathlib:DifferentiableOn`.

Proposed home: `TauCeti/Analysis/Complex/TaylorPowerSeries`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

**Sources.**

- [STANLEY.EC1](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/ec1.pdf), Section 1.1, p. 13 (the informal principle after Example 1.1.5) and pp. 14 and 17 (power series that agree near 0 have equal coefficients): Stanley states the converse principle informally: an identity of convergent series persists as a formal identity. The node proves the opposite direction, a formal identity giving an analytic identity on a disc where the denominator has no zero, which Stanley does not state; pp. 14 and 17 supply the uniqueness of coefficients the proof uses.
- [nist-dlmf-2026](https://dlmf.nist.gov/24.2), §24.2(i), (24.2.1): A formal identity (Mathlib's bernoulliPowerSeries_mul_exp_sub_one) valid analytically on a disc limited by the nearest zero of the denominator; the theorem is the general form of this specialisation.

<a id="CA-2-bernoulli-coefficients-do-not-decay"></a>

#### CA.2.31 The Bernoulli series diverges on and beyond |z| = 2π

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/bernoulli-coefficients-do-not-decay` · lemma · CA.2 continuation packet

(a) For k ≥ 1: |B_{2k}|·(2π)^{2k}/(2k)! = 2ζ(2k) ≥ 2. (b) For z ∈ ℂ with |z| ≥ 2π, the terms B_n zⁿ/n! do not tend to 0, so Σ_n B_n zⁿ/n! is not summable (Mathlib's bernoulli, B₁ = −1/2).

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- k ≥ 1 in (a); |z| ≥ 2π in (b). This includes the boundary circle, which the analytic theorem's radius statement leaves open.

**Checks.**

- k = 1: |B₂|(2π)²/2! = (1/6)·4π²/2 = π²/3 = 2ζ(2).
- Together with CA.2/bernoulli-generating-function-on-its-disc this pins the radius at exactly 2π and decides the boundary circle (divergent), which the parent signature not_summable_bernoulli_mul_pow (strict 2π < |z|) leaves open.

**Proof sketch.**

1. (a) Mathlib's hasSum_zeta_nat: Σ_{n≥1} 1/n^{2k} = (−1)^{k+1}2^{2k−1}π^{2k}B_{2k}/(2k)!; the left side is ζ(2k) > 1, so (−1)^{k+1}B_{2k} > 0 and |B_{2k}|(2π)^{2k}/(2k)! = 2ζ(2k) ≥ 2 (DLMF (24.9.8) gives the slightly stronger lower bound 2/(1 − 2^{−2k})).
2. (b) For |z| ≥ 2π, |B_{2k}z^{2k}/(2k)!| ≥ |B_{2k}|(2π)^{2k}/(2k)! ≥ 2 for every k ≥ 1, so the terms do not tend to 0 (Summable.tendsto_atTop_zero, the additive form of Multipliable.tendsto_atTop_one).

**Needs:** `mathlib:hasSum_zeta_nat`, `mathlib:bernoulli`, `mathlib:Multipliable.tendsto_atTop_one`.

Proposed home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/ClassicalArithmetic/CA2`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

**Sources.**

- [nist-dlmf-24-9](https://dlmf.nist.gov/24.9), §24.9, (24.9.8), retrieved 2026-10-14: For n ≥ 1, bounds (−1)^{n+1}B_{2n} below by 2(2n)!/(2π)^{2n} times 1/(1 − 2^{−2n}), and above by the same quantity times 1/(1 − 2^{β−2n}) with β = 2 + log₂(1 − 6/π²) ≈ 0.649 (24.9.9).

<a id="CA-2-bernoulli-generating-function-on-its-disc"></a>

#### CA.2.32 The Bernoulli generating function on its disc of convergence

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/bernoulli-generating-function-on-its-disc` · theorem

For z ∈ ℂ with |z| < 2π: ∑\_{n≥0} B_n zⁿ/n! = z/(e^z − 1) for z ≠ 0 and = 1 for z = 0, with Mathlib's `bernoulli` (B₁ = −1/2). The radius 2π is exact: the series diverges for |z| > 2π.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- Mathlib's convention B₁ = −1/2 (`bernoulli`); with `bernoulli'` (B₁ = +1/2) the sum is z e^z/(e^z − 1).

**Checks.**

- At z = 0 the sum is B₀ = 1.
- Numerically at z = 1: ∑ Bₙ/n! = 1/(e − 1) ≈ 0.58198.
- DLMF 24.2.1 states exactly this with |t| < 2π.

**Proof sketch.**

1. Let g(z) = (e^z − 1)/z for z ≠ 0 and g(0) = 1, that is g = dslope (exp − 1) 0, which is entire (`Complex.differentiableOn_dslope`).
2. g(z) = 0 iff e^z = 1 and z ≠ 0, iff z ∈ 2πiℤ ∖ {0} (`Complex.exp_eq_one_iff`); so g has no zero on |z| < 2π.
3. X·T(g) = T(z·g) = T(e^z − 1) = exp − 1 formally (taylor-series-of-a-complex-function); Mathlib's bernoulliPowerSeries ℂ · (exp − 1) = X, so bernoulliPowerSeries·X·T(g) = X and, cancelling X in the domain ℂ⟦X⟧, bernoulliPowerSeries·T(g) = 1 = T(1).
4. Apply formal-identities-specialise-on-a-disc with h = 1 and r = 2π: ∑ B_n zⁿ/n! = 1/g(z).
5. Exactness of the radius: a power series converging at some |z₀| > 2π would define a holomorphic function on |z| < |z₀| equal to 1/g near 0, hence bounded near 2πi, but 1/g has a pole at 2πi.

**Needs:** [CA.2/taylor-series-of-a-complex-function](#CA-2-taylor-series-of-a-complex-function), [CA.2/formal-identities-specialise-on-a-disc](#CA-2-formal-identities-specialise-on-a-disc), `mathlib:bernoulli`, `mathlib:bernoulliPowerSeries`, `mathlib:bernoulliPowerSeries_mul_exp_sub_one`, `mathlib:Complex.exp_eq_one_iff`, `mathlib:dslope`, `mathlib:Complex.differentiableOn_dslope`, [CA.2/bernoulli-coefficients-do-not-decay](#CA-2-bernoulli-coefficients-do-not-decay).

It strengthens the signature not_summable_bernoulli_mul_pow (2π < |z|) to 2π ≤ |z|. Suppliers: [CA.2/bernoulli-coefficients-do-not-decay](#CA-2-bernoulli-coefficients-do-not-decay).

<a id="CA-2-tangent-coefficients-do-not-decay"></a>

#### CA.2.33 The secant-plus-tangent series diverges on and beyond |z| = π/2

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/tangent-coefficients-do-not-decay` · lemma · CA.2 continuation packet

Let e : ℕ → ℚ be any sequence whose odd terms are the tangent numbers in their Bernoulli closed form, e(2n + 1) = (−1)ⁿ2^{2n+2}(2^{2n+2} − 1)B_{2n+2}/(2n + 2) (for the Euler zigzag numbers this is the API item zigzag_odd_eq_bernoulli of CA.2/euler-zigzag-numbers). Then for z ∈ ℂ with |z| ≥ π/2 the terms e(n)zⁿ/n! do not tend to 0, so Σ_n e(n)zⁿ/n! is not summable.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- |z| ≥ π/2; only the odd terms of e are constrained.

**Checks.**

- k = 1: e(1) = 1 and (4/π)(3/4)ζ(2) = π/2 = 1·(π/2)¹/1!.
- k = 2: e(3) = 2 from B₄ = −1/30, and 2(π/2)³/3! = π³/24 = (4/π)(15/16)ζ(4).

**Proof sketch.**

1. With k = n + 1, |e(2k − 1)|/(2k − 1)! = 2^{2k}(2^{2k} − 1)|B_{2k}|/(2k)! = 2(2^{2k} − 1)ζ(2k)/π^{2k} by bernoulli-coefficients-do-not-decay (a).
2. Hence |e(2k − 1)|(π/2)^{2k−1}/(2k − 1)! = (4/π)(1 − 2^{−2k})ζ(2k) ≥ 3/π for every k ≥ 1, and for |z| ≥ π/2 the odd terms have absolute value at least 3/π; the terms do not tend to 0.

**Needs:** [CA.2/bernoulli-coefficients-do-not-decay](#CA-2-bernoulli-coefficients-do-not-decay), `mathlib:bernoulli`, `mathlib:Multipliable.tendsto_atTop_one`.

Proposed home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/ClassicalArithmetic/CA2`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

<a id="CA-2-secant-plus-tangent-on-its-disc"></a>

#### CA.2.34 sec + tan on its disc of convergence

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/secant-plus-tangent-on-its-disc` · theorem

For z ∈ ℂ with |z| < π/2: ∑\_{n≥0} E_n zⁿ/n! = 1/cos z + tan z. The radius π/2 is exact.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- tan z = sin z / cos z (Mathlib's `Complex.tan`); cos z ≠ 0 on the disc.

**Checks.**

- Even part sec z, odd part tan z (DLMF 4.19.5 and 4.19.3, both on |z| < π/2).
- z = 0 gives E₀ = 1.

**Proof sketch.**

1. cos z = 0 iff z = (2k + 1)π/2 (`Complex.cos_eq_zero_iff`), so cos has no zero on |z| < π/2.
2. The formal identity (∑ E_n Xⁿ/n!)·T(cos) = T(1 + sin) holds by secant-plus-tangent-formal-identity and T(cos) = cos X, T(sin) = sin X (taylor-series-of-a-complex-function).
3. Apply formal-identities-specialise-on-a-disc with g = cos, h = 1 + sin: the sum is (1 + sin z)/cos z = 1/cos z + tan z (`Complex.tan_eq_sin_div_cos`).
4. The radius is exact because (1 + sin z)/cos z has a pole at z = π/2, where 1 + sin z = 2 (at z = −π/2 the singularity is removable: (1 + sin z)/cos z = cos z/(1 − sin z) there).

**Needs:** [CA.2/secant-plus-tangent-formal-identity](#CA-2-secant-plus-tangent-formal-identity), [CA.2/taylor-series-of-a-complex-function](#CA-2-taylor-series-of-a-complex-function), [CA.2/formal-identities-specialise-on-a-disc](#CA-2-formal-identities-specialise-on-a-disc), `mathlib:Complex.cos_eq_zero_iff`, `mathlib:Complex.tan_eq_sin_div_cos`, `mathlib:Complex.cos`, `mathlib:Complex.tan`, [CA.2/tangent-coefficients-do-not-decay](#CA-2-tangent-coefficients-do-not-decay).

### Eulerian numbers

Eulerian numbers counted by descents, their identities and unimodality, and the inequalities of Lawrence–Sawin's Appendix C at their exact ranges.

<a id="CA-2-eulerian-numbers"></a>

#### CA.2.35 Eulerian numbers

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/eulerian-numbers` · definition · planet: **Eulerian numbers** · CA.2 continuation packet

For n, q ∈ ℕ, the Eulerian number A(n, q) is the number of permutations σ of {1, …, n} with exactly q descents, a descent being a position i with 1 ≤ i < n and σ(i) > σ(i + 1). In Lean the permutations are Equiv.Perm (Fin n) and descentCount σ counts the positions i : Fin n with i + 1 < n and σ(i + 1) < σ(i). The empty permutation has no descent, so A(0, 0) = 1 and A(0, q) = 0 for q ≥ 1; for n ≥ 1, A(n, q) = 0 for q ≥ n. The count by ascents (σ(i) < σ(i + 1)) gives the same numbers. In Stanley's indexing A_Stanley(d, k) = A(d, k − 1) (his k counts 1 + des), and Lawrence–Sawin's A(n, q) is this A(n, q).

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- n and q are natural numbers; no range condition is built into the definition, the vanishing outside 0 ≤ q < n (n ≥ 1) is a theorem.
- The zero-degree value A(0, 0) = 1 is the count of the empty permutation. It is kept separate from Lawrence–Sawin's convention 'A(n, q) = 0 unless 0 ≤ q < n', which they use only for n ≥ 1, and from Stanley's convention A_Stanley(0, k) = δ_{0k} (that is A₀(x) = 1), which is a separate normalisation of his shifted indexing at d = 0 and does not correspond to A(0, 0) under k = q + 1; the identities planned here (row sums, Worpitzky at m = q + 1 ≥ 1) hold with A(0, 0) = 1.

**API.**

- `eulerian` (data): A(n, q) := #{σ ∈ Equiv.Perm (Fin n) : descentCount σ = q}.
- `descentCount` (data): The number of positions i with i + 1 < n and σ(i + 1) < σ(i).
- `ascentCount` (data): The number of positions i with i + 1 < n and σ(i) < σ(i + 1).
- `eulerian_zero_zero` (simp): A(0, 0) = 1.
- `eulerian_zero_right` (simp): A(n, 0) = 1 for every n (only the identity has no descent).
- `eulerian_eq_zero_of_le` (simp): For 1 ≤ n ≤ q, A(n, q) = 0.
- `eulerian_one_right` (example): A(n, 1) = 2ⁿ − n − 1 (natural subtraction; both sides 0 for n ≤ 1).
- `card_ascentCount_eq_eulerian` (characterisation): \#{σ : ascentCount σ = q} = A(n, q): complementing values σ ↦ (n + 1 − σ) exchanges ascents and descents.

**Unit tests.**

- `eulerian_three_one` (computation): A(3, 1) = 4 (the permutations 132, 213, 231, 312).
- `eulerian_four_row` (computation): A(4, 0) = 1, A(4, 1) = 11, A(4, 2) = 11, A(4, 3) = 1.
- `eulerian_two_row` (computation): A(2, 0) = A(2, 1) = 1.
- `sum_eulerian_zero` (degenerate): Σ_{q ≤ 0} A(0, q) = 0! = 1, that is A(0, 0) = 1: a definition that builds in 'A(n, q) = 0 unless q < n' gives 0 here and breaks the row sum.
- `sum_eulerian_five` (compatibility): Σ_{q ≤ 5} A(5, q) = 120 = Nat.factorial 5.
- `eulerian_ne_zigzag` (non-example): A(3, 1) = 4 ≠ 2 = E₃: Eulerian numbers are not the Euler zigzag numbers of CA.2/euler-zigzag-numbers, nor counts of Eulerian circuits in graphs.

**Checks.**

- A(4, ·) = 1, 11, 11, 1 and A(5, ·) = 1, 26, 66, 26, 1 (Stanley's table of Eulerian polynomials).
- A(0, 0) = 1, so the row sums are n! for every n ≥ 0, including n = 0.

**Construction and proof.**

1. Define descentCount σ as the cardinality of the finite set of positions i : Fin n with i + 1 < n and σ(i + 1) < σ(i), and A(n, q) as the cardinality of {σ ∈ Equiv.Perm (Fin n) : descentCount σ = q}.
2. The basic identities (sum n!, symmetry, recurrence, Worpitzky) are proved in eulerian-basic-identities; this node fixes the object and its conventions.

**Uses.**

- Lawrence–Sawin, Lemma 3.4, p. 20: the Euler characteristics χ(H, Ω^i_H) of an ample hypersurface of degree d in an abelian variety of dimension n are ±d·A(n, i); that Hodge interpretation stays with the hypersurface owner
- Lawrence–Sawin, Appendix B (Propositions B.1 and B.11 and their lemmas), pp. 93–116: the numerical elimination of exceptional monodromy groups compares products of Eulerian numbers with binomial counts, through the bounds of Appendix C
- CA.2/eulerian-power-bounds, eulerian-small-descent-bounds, eulerian-square-separation, eulerian-ratio-bound: the inequalities of Lemmas C.1–C.5 are stated for this A(n, q)

**Needs:** `mathlib:Equiv.Perm`, `mathlib:Finset.card`, `mathlib:Finset.filter`.

Proposed home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/ClassicalArithmetic/CA2`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

**Sources.**

- [STANLEY.EC1](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/ec1.pdf), §1.4, (1.36) and the paragraph after it, p. 39: Defines A(d, k) as the number of permutations of [d] with k − 1 descents, the Eulerian polynomial A_d(x) = Σ_w x^{1+des(w)}, sets A(0, k) = δ_{0k} and tabulates A_0(x), …, A_8(x).
- [lawrence-sawin-2025](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.09046v5), §3, Lemma 3.4, p. 20; Appendix B, opening paragraph, p. 93; Appendix C, proof of Lemma C.1, p. 116: Uses A(n, i) for the Eulerian number in the Hodge-number formula, adopts the convention A(n, q) = 0 unless 0 ≤ q < n, and recalls that A(n, q) counts permutations of {1, …, n} with exactly q ascents.

<a id="CA-2-eulerian-basic-identities"></a>

#### CA.2.36 Basic identities of Eulerian numbers

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/eulerian-basic-identities` · theorem · CA.2 continuation packet

For all n, q ∈ ℕ: (a) Σ_{q=0}^{n} A(n, q) = n!; (b) for q < n, A(n, q) = A(n, n − 1 − q); (c) A(n + 1, q + 1) = (q + 2)·A(n, q + 1) + (n − q)·A(n, q), with natural subtraction (for q ≥ n both sides vanish); (d) Worpitzky's identity (q + 1)ⁿ = Σ_{j=0}^{q} A(n, j)·C(n + q − j, n); (e) A(n, 0) = 1 and A(n, 1) = 2ⁿ − n − 1; (f) the number of permutations with q ascents is A(n, q).

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- n, q ∈ ℕ; (b) needs q < n, which forces n ≥ 1.

**Checks.**

- Row 5 is 1, 26, 66, 26, 1, summing to 120 and symmetric.
- Worpitzky at n = 2, q = 1: 4 = A(2, 0)·C(3, 2) + A(2, 1)·C(2, 2) = 3 + 1.
- The recurrence at n = 2, q = 0: A(3, 1) = 2·A(2, 1) + 2·A(2, 0) = 4.

**Proof sketch.**

1. (a) The sets {σ : des σ = q}, 0 ≤ q ≤ n, partition Equiv.Perm (Fin n), whose cardinality is n! (Fintype.card_perm).
2. (b) and (f): reversal σ ↦ σ ∘ rev sends a permutation with q descents to one with n − 1 − q descents, and complementation σ ↦ rev ∘ σ exchanges descents and ascents (Stanley p. 40, the paragraph before Proposition 1.4.3).
3. (c) Insert n + 1 into a permutation of [n]: inserting it into a descent slot or at the end keeps the descent number, inserting it into an ascent slot or at the front raises it by one; this is Stanley's recurrence (1.39) A(d + 1, k) = kA(d, k) + (d − k + 2)A(d, k − 1) with k = q + 2.
4. (d) For n ≥ 1, Stanley's Proposition 1.4.4 gives Σ_{m≥0} mⁿxᵐ = A_n(x)/(1 − x)^{n+1} with A_n(x) = Σ_j A(n, j)x^{j+1}; expanding 1/(1 − x)^{n+1} = Σ_k C(n + k, n)x^k (Mathlib's PowerSeries.invOneSubPow) and comparing coefficients of x^{q+1} gives (d). At n = 0 Stanley sets A₀(x) = 1 rather than x, so (d) is checked directly there: only j = 0 contributes, and both sides are 1 because A(0, 0) = 1.
5. (e) A(n, 0) = 1 because only the identity has no descent; A(n, 1) = 2ⁿ − n − 1 follows from (d) at q = 1: 2ⁿ = A(n, 0)C(n + 1, n) + A(n, 1).

**Needs:** [CA.2/eulerian-numbers](#CA-2-eulerian-numbers), `mathlib:Fintype.card_perm`, `mathlib:Nat.choose`, `mathlib:PowerSeries.invOneSubPow`, `mathlib:Fin.revPerm`.

**Sources.**

- [STANLEY.EC1](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/ec1.pdf), §1.4, the paragraph before Proposition 1.4.3 and Propositions 1.4.3–1.4.4 with the proof of 1.4.4, (1.37)–(1.39), p. 40: Shows that reversal turns d − 1 − j descents into j descents, proves Σ m^d x^m = A_d(x)/(1 − x)^{d+1} by induction through the recurrence (1.39), and proves (1.39) by inserting d + 1 into a permutation of [d].
- [lawrence-sawin-2025](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.09046v5), Appendix C, Lemmas C.1–C.2 with their proofs, p. 116; Appendix A, proof of Lemma A.6, p. 92; Appendix B, opening paragraph, p. 93: The proof of Lemma C.2 is the factorial sum Σ_q A(n, q) = n!; the proof of Lemma A.6 uses the symmetry A(n, k) = A(n, n − 1 − k); the proof of Lemma C.1 recalls that A(n, q) counts the permutations with exactly q ascents; the opening of Appendix B fixes the convention A(n, q) = 0 outside 0 ≤ q < n.

<a id="CA-2-eulerian-unimodal"></a>

#### CA.2.37 Unimodality of the rows of Eulerian numbers

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/eulerian-unimodal` · lemma · CA.2 continuation packet

For n ∈ ℕ and q with 2(q + 1) ≤ n − 1: A(n, q) ≤ A(n, q + 1). With the symmetry A(n, q) = A(n, n − 1 − q), each row A(n, 0), …, A(n, n − 1) rises weakly to its middle and falls symmetrically after it.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- 2(q + 1) ≤ n − 1 means q + 1 ≤ (n − 1)/2, the left half of the row; for n = 0 the hypothesis never holds.

**Checks.**

- Row 6 is 1, 57, 302, 302, 57, 1; row 7 is 1, 120, 1191, 2416, 1191, 120, 1.
- Checked numerically for every n ≤ 70 and every q in the range.

**Proof sketch.**

1. Induction on n with the recurrence of eulerian-basic-identities (c): A(n, q + 1) − A(n, q) = (q + 2)A(n − 1, q + 1) + (n − 2q − 2)A(n − 1, q) − (n − q)A(n − 1, q − 1) for 1 ≤ q (and the analogous expression at q = 0).
2. Under 2(q + 1) ≤ n − 1 the index q + 1 is at most the middle (n − 2)/2 of row n − 1, or equals it up to the symmetric partner when n is odd; by the induction hypothesis and the symmetry, A(n − 1, q + 1) ≥ A(n − 1, q) ≥ A(n − 1, q − 1).
3. Hence the difference is at least ((q + 2) + (n − 2q − 2) − (n − q))·A(n − 1, q − 1) = 0, all coefficients other than the last being nonnegative because n − 2q − 2 ≥ 1.
4. Alternatively (Stanley, Exercise 1.50(e) with its solution): the Eulerian polynomial has only real zeros (Exercise 1.49), hence log-concave coefficients by Newton's inequalities, hence unimodal; symmetry places the peak in the middle.

**Needs:** [CA.2/eulerian-basic-identities](#CA-2-eulerian-basic-identities).

Proposed home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/ClassicalArithmetic/CA2`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

**Sources.**

- [STANLEY.EC1](https://math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/ec1.pdf), Chapter 1, Exercise 1.50(e), p. 124, with its solution, p. 178; Exercises 1.49 and 1.50(a)–(b), p. 124, with the solutions of 1.49 and 1.50(b), p. 177: Asks to show that Σ_{w ∈ S_n} x^{des(w)} is symmetric and unimodal, and solves it from the real-rootedness of the Eulerian polynomial (Exercise 1.49) and Newton's inequalities (Exercise 1.50(a),(b)); cites Gasharov for a combinatorial proof.
- [lawrence-sawin-2025](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.09046v5), Appendix C, proof of Lemma C.4, p. 117: Uses, without stating it as a lemma, that A(n, r) ≥ A(n, r₀) for r₀ ≤ r ≤ n/2, which is this unimodality.

<a id="CA-2-eulerian-power-bounds"></a>

#### CA.2.38 Power and factorial bounds for Eulerian numbers (Lawrence–Sawin, Lemmas C.1–C.2)

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/eulerian-power-bounds` · theorem · CA.2 continuation packet

For n ≥ 1 and q ≥ 0: (q + 1)ⁿ − (n + 1)qⁿ ≤ A(n, q) ≤ (q + 1)ⁿ (the left side computed in ℤ), and A(n, q) ≤ n!. The upper bound (q + 1)ⁿ and A(n, q) ≤ n! hold for n = 0 as well.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- n ≥ 1 for the lower bound, as in the source; q ∈ ℕ arbitrary (for q ≥ n the bounds are consistent with A(n, q) = 0).

**Checks.**

- n = 3, q = 1: 2³ − 4·1 = 4 ≤ A(3, 1) = 4 ≤ 8: the lower bound is attained.
- n = 4, q = 2: 3⁴ − 5·2⁴ = 1 ≤ 11 ≤ 81.
- For q ≥ n the lower bound is ≤ 0, consistent with A(n, q) = 0 (checked for n ≤ 70, q ≤ n + 2).

**Proof sketch.**

1. Upper bound: by Worpitzky's identity (eulerian-basic-identities (d)) (q + 1)ⁿ is a sum of nonnegative terms one of which is A(n, q)·C(n, n) = A(n, q). (Lawrence–Sawin's argument: labelling [n] by 1, …, q + 1 and listing each label class in decreasing order gives every permutation with at most q ascents.)
2. Lower bound (Lawrence–Sawin's argument): the labellings producing a permutation with fewer than q ascents have two adjacent labels whose classes are separated; recording the position j ∈ {0, …, n} of the cut and merging the labels injects them into (n + 1)·qⁿ data, so the number of permutations with exactly q ascents is at least (q + 1)ⁿ − (n + 1)qⁿ.
3. A(n, q) ≤ n! from Σ_q A(n, q) = n! (eulerian-basic-identities (a)).
4. Ascents and descents give the same numbers (eulerian-basic-identities (f)), so the source's ascent count is A(n, q).

**Needs:** [CA.2/eulerian-basic-identities](#CA-2-eulerian-basic-identities).

Proposed home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/ClassicalArithmetic/CA2`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

**Sources.**

- [lawrence-sawin-2025](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.09046v5), Appendix C, Lemma C.1 with its proof, p. 116: States (q + 1)ⁿ − (n + 1)qⁿ ≤ A(n, q) ≤ (q + 1)ⁿ for n ≥ 1, q ≥ 0, and proves both halves by the labelling argument.
- [lawrence-sawin-2025](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.09046v5), Appendix C, Lemma C.2 with its proof, p. 116: States A(n, q) ≤ n! and derives it from the factorial sum.

<a id="CA-2-eulerian-small-descent-bounds"></a>

#### CA.2.39 Eulerian numbers with few descents (Lawrence–Sawin, Lemma C.3)

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/eulerian-small-descent-bounds` · theorem · CA.2 continuation packet

For n ≥ 2 and q ∈ ℕ with q < n/(log(n + 1) + 1) − 1 (natural logarithm, real comparison): (1 − 1/e)(q + 1)ⁿ ≤ A(n, q) ≤ (q + 1)ⁿ.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- n ≥ 2; the hypothesis on q is the real inequality q + 1 < n/(log(n + 1) + 1).

**Checks.**

- n = 20: log 21 + 1 ≈ 4.04, so q ≤ 3 is allowed; A(20, 3) ≥ (1 − 1/e)·4²⁰.
- Checked numerically for n ≤ 70 and every admissible q.

**Proof sketch.**

1. From 1/(q + 1) < log((q + 1)/q) for q ≥ 1, ((q + 1)/q)ⁿ > e^{n/(q+1)}; the hypothesis n/(q + 1) > log(n + 1) + 1 gives ((q + 1)/q)ⁿ > e(n + 1), that is (n + 1)qⁿ < (q + 1)ⁿ/e (trivially true at q = 0).
2. Insert this into the lower bound of eulerian-power-bounds: A(n, q) ≥ (q + 1)ⁿ − (n + 1)qⁿ > (1 − 1/e)(q + 1)ⁿ; the upper bound is the upper half of that node.

**Needs:** [CA.2/eulerian-power-bounds](#CA-2-eulerian-power-bounds), `mathlib:Real.log`, `mathlib:Real.exp`, `mathlib:Real.add_one_le_exp`.

Proposed home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/ClassicalArithmetic/CA2`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

**Sources.**

- [lawrence-sawin-2025](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.09046v5), Appendix C, Lemma C.3 with its proof, pp. 116–117: States the bound (1 − 1/e)(q + 1)ⁿ ≤ A(n, q) ≤ (q + 1)ⁿ for n ≥ 2 and q < n/(log(n + 1) + 1) − 1, proved from the logarithm inequalities and Lemma C.1.

<a id="CA-2-eulerian-square-separation"></a>

#### CA.2.40 A product inequality for Eulerian numbers (Lawrence–Sawin, Lemma C.4)

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/eulerian-square-separation` · theorem · CA.2 continuation packet

For n ∈ ℕ and 3 ≤ r ≤ n − 2: A(n, r − 1)·(A(n, r − 1) − 1) > 2·A(n, 3r − 2).

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- 3 ≤ r ≤ n − 2, which forces n ≥ 5; for 3r − 2 ≥ n the right side is 0.

**Checks.**

- n = 5, r = 3: A(5, 2)(A(5, 2) − 1) = 66·65 > 0 = 2A(5, 7).
- n = 12, r = 3: A(12, 2) = 478 271 and A(12, 7) = 66 318 474, so the left side ≈ 2.29·10¹¹ exceeds 2A(12, 7) ≈ 1.33·10⁸.
- Checked numerically for every n ≤ 70 and 3 ≤ r ≤ n − 2.

**Proof sketch.**

1. Small n: for n ≤ 20 the finitely many cases are checked by computation (the source's ancillary Python code, bound-B; rechecked here for all n ≤ 70).
2. Assume n ≥ 21 and r ≤ n/2 (for r > n/2, 3r − 2 ≥ n and the right side vanishes). There is an integer r₀ with √n ≤ r₀ < n/(log(n + 1) + 1), so either r < n/(log(n + 1) + 1) or r ≥ r₀.
3. If r < n/(log(n + 1) + 1): eulerian-small-descent-bounds gives A(n, r − 1) ≥ (1 − 1/e)rⁿ, and eulerian-power-bounds gives 2A(n, 3r − 2) ≤ 2(3r − 1)ⁿ; and (1 − 1/e)²r^{2n} > 2(3r − 1)ⁿ + (1 − 1/e)rⁿ for r ≥ 3, n ≥ 14.
4. If r ≥ r₀: by eulerian-unimodal A(n, r − 1) ≥ A(n, r₀ − 1) (r − 1 ≤ n/2 − 1 is in the rising half), and eulerian-small-descent-bounds at r₀ − 1 gives A(n, r₀ − 1)(A(n, r₀ − 1) − 1) > (3/10)r₀^{2n} ≥ (3/10)nⁿ > 2·n! ≥ 2A(n, 3r − 2) by eulerian-power-bounds (A ≤ n!).

**Needs:** [CA.2/eulerian-small-descent-bounds](#CA-2-eulerian-small-descent-bounds), [CA.2/eulerian-power-bounds](#CA-2-eulerian-power-bounds), [CA.2/eulerian-unimodal](#CA-2-eulerian-unimodal).

Proposed home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/ClassicalArithmetic/CA2`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

**Sources.**

- [lawrence-sawin-2025](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.09046v5), Appendix C, Lemma C.4 with its proof, p. 117: States A(n, r − 1)(A(n, r − 1) − 1) > 2A(n, 3r − 2) for 3 ≤ r ≤ n − 2 and proves it for n ≥ 21 by the two-case argument above, leaving n ≤ 20 to the ancillary code; the second case uses the monotonicity A(n, r) ≥ A(n, r₀) without naming it.

<a id="CA-2-eulerian-ratio-bound"></a>

#### CA.2.41 The ratio A(n, 2)/A(n, 1)² (Lawrence–Sawin, Lemma C.5)

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/eulerian-ratio-bound` · theorem · CA.2 continuation packet

For n ≥ 11: 27·A(n, 2) < A(n, 1)², i.e. A(n, 2)/A(n, 1)² < 1/27. The threshold is sharp: at n = 10, A(10, 1) = 1013 and A(10, 2) = 47 840, so 27·47 840 = 1 291 680 > 1 026 169 = 1013².

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- n ≥ 11.

**Checks.**

- The inequality fails for 3 ≤ n ≤ 10 (checked), so the hypothesis n ≥ 11 cannot be weakened.
- Checked numerically for n ≤ 70.

**Proof sketch.**

1. eulerian-power-bounds gives A(n, 2) ≤ 3ⁿ, and for n ≥ 6 eulerian-small-descent-bounds at q = 1 gives A(n, 1) ≥ (1 − 1/e)2ⁿ (its hypothesis 1 < n/(log(n + 1) + 1) − 1 holds from n = 6).
2. Hence 27A(n, 2)/A(n, 1)² ≤ 27(3/4)ⁿ/(1 − 1/e)², which is < 1 for n ≥ 15.
3. The cases 11 ≤ n ≤ 14 are checked directly from A(n, 1) = 2ⁿ − n − 1 and the recurrence (e.g. n = 11: A(11, 1) = 2036, A(11, 2) = 152 637, and 27·152 637 = 4 121 199 < 4 145 296).

**Needs:** [CA.2/eulerian-small-descent-bounds](#CA-2-eulerian-small-descent-bounds), [CA.2/eulerian-power-bounds](#CA-2-eulerian-power-bounds), [CA.2/eulerian-basic-identities](#CA-2-eulerian-basic-identities).

### Generalised binomial coefficients and p-free factorials

Yu's binomial arithmetic: divisibility of generalised binomial coefficients, the p-free factorial with its binomial factorisations, and the Luo–Zhu congruence.

<a id="CA-2-generalized-binomial-divisibility"></a>

#### CA.2.42 Divisibility of generalised binomial coefficients (Yu, Lemme 7.2.2)

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/generalized-binomial-divisibility` · theorem · CA.2 continuation packet

For a nonzero integer n and an integer m ≥ 1, n/gcd(n, m) divides the generalised binomial coefficient C(n, m) = n(n − 1)···(n − m + 1)/m! (Mathlib's Ring.choose on ℤ), negative upper entries included. The supporting absorption identity: for every n ∈ ℤ and m ∈ ℕ, (m + 1)·C(n, m + 1) = n·C(n − 1, m).

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- n ∈ ℤ, n ≠ 0; m ∈ ℕ, m ≥ 1. For m > n ≥ 1, C(n, m) = 0 and the statement is trivial.

**Checks.**

- n = −2, m = 2: C(−2, 2) = 3 and n/gcd = −1.
- n = −4, m = 2: C(−4, 2) = 10 and n/gcd = −2 divides it.
- The gcd cannot be dropped: 4 ∤ C(4, 2) = 6.
- Checked for every 0 < |n| ≤ 40 and 1 ≤ m ≤ 29.

**Proof sketch.**

1. Absorption: multiply both sides by m! and use Ring.descPochhammer_eq_factorial_smul_choose: (m + 1)!·C(n, m + 1) is the falling factorial n(n − 1)···(n − m) = n·[(n − 1)···(n − m)] = n·m!·C(n − 1, m); cancel m! in the torsion-free ℤ.
2. Write g = gcd(n, m), n = g·n′, m = g·m′ with gcd(n′, m′) = 1. Absorption at m − 1 gives m·C(n, m) = n·C(n − 1, m − 1), so m′·C(n, m) = n′·C(n − 1, m − 1) is divisible by n′.
3. Since gcd(m′, n′) = 1, n′ divides C(n, m) (Int.dvd_of_dvd_mul_right_of_gcd_one).

**Needs:** `mathlib:Ring.choose`, `mathlib:Ring.choose_neg`, `mathlib:Ring.descPochhammer_eq_factorial_smul_choose`, `mathlib:Int.dvd_of_dvd_mul_right_of_gcd_one`.

Proposed home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/ClassicalArithmetic/CA2`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

**Sources.**

- [yu-2023](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.04659v5), §7.2.2, Lemme 7.2.2 with its proof, p. 67 (arXiv v5): States that n/(n, m) divides the binomial coefficient C(n, m) for nonzero integers n, m with m ≥ 1, and proves it from (m/n)C(n, m) = C(n − 1, m − 1) and the coprimality of m/(m, n) and n/(m, n).

<a id="CA-2-p-free-factorial"></a>

#### CA.2.43 The p-free factorial

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/p-free-factorial` · definition · CA.2 continuation packet

For a natural number p and N ∈ ℕ, the p-free factorial f_p(N) is the product of the integers 1 ≤ i ≤ N with p ∤ i; f_p(0) = 1 (empty product). For p prime, N! = p^{⌊N/p⌋}·⌊N/p⌋!·f_p(N) and f_p(N) is prime to p (a p-adic unit). Negative arguments are not part of the definition.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- p, N ∈ ℕ; the factorial split holds for every p (for p = 0 and p = 1 it degenerates to N! = N! and N! = N!·1), while the unit property needs p prime.

**API.**

- `pFreeFactorial` (data): f_p(N) := ∏\_{1 ≤ i ≤ N, p ∤ i} i.
- `pFreeFactorial_zero` (simp): f_p(0) = 1.
- `pFreeFactorial_succ` (simp): f_p(N + 1) = f_p(N)·(1 if p ∣ N + 1, else N + 1).
- `factorial_eq_mul_pFreeFactorial` (characterisation): N! = p^{⌊N/p⌋}·⌊N/p⌋!·f_p(N), for every p.
- `not_dvd_pFreeFactorial` (relation): For p prime, p ∤ f_p(N).
- `pFreeFactorial_prime` (example): For p prime, f_p(p) = (p − 1)!, so f_p(p) ≡ −1 (mod p) by Wilson's theorem (ZMod.wilsons_lemma).

**Unit tests.**

- `pFreeFactorial_three_six` (computation): f_3(6) = 40.
- `pFreeFactorial_two_four` (computation): f_2(4) = 3.
- `pFreeFactorial_zero` (degenerate): f_p(0) = 1 for every p.
- `pFreeFactorial_ne_ordCompl` (non-example): f_2(6) = 15 ≠ 45 = 6!/2^{v₂(6!)}: the p-free factorial is not the prime-to-p part of N!, which also removes the p-free part of ⌊N/p⌋!.
- `factorial_six_eq_mul_pFreeFactorial` (compatibility): With Mathlib's Nat.factorial: 6! = 3²·2!·f_3(6) = 9·2·40.

**Checks.**

- f_3(6) = 1·2·4·5 = 40; f_2(4) = 1·3 = 3; f_5(5) = 4! = 24 ≡ −1 (mod 5).
- f_p(N) is not the prime-to-p part of N!: f_2(6) = 15 while 6! = 2⁴·45.

**Construction and proof.**

1. Define f_p(N) := ∏ over i ∈ Icc 1 N with ¬ p ∣ i of i.
2. Factorial split: the multiples of p up to N are p·1, …, p·⌊N/p⌋, whose product is p^{⌊N/p⌋}·⌊N/p⌋!; the other factors give f_p(N) (Finset.prod_filter_mul_prod_filter_not).
3. Unit property: a product of integers prime to p is prime to p (Nat.Prime.coprime_iff_not_dvd and Nat.coprime_prod_left_iff).

**Uses.**

- Yu, proof of Théorème 7.2.3, pp. 71–72: the ratios f_p(np)/(f_p(mp)f_p((n − m)p)) and f_p(np + mp)/(f_p(mp)f_p(np)) carry the p-adic unit part of binomial coefficients of multiples of p
- CA.2/luo-zhu-congruence: the congruence f_p(p^αN) ≡ f_p(p^α)^N is stated for f_p
- CA.2/p-free-factorial-binomial-factorisation: the binomial factorisations are stated with f_p

**Needs:** `mathlib:Finset.prod`, `mathlib:Finset.Icc`, `mathlib:Nat.factorial`, `mathlib:Finset.prod_filter_mul_prod_filter_not`, `mathlib:Nat.coprime_prod_left_iff`, `mathlib:Nat.Prime.coprime_iff_not_dvd`.

Proposed home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/ClassicalArithmetic/CA2`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

**Sources.**

- [yu-2023](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.04659v5), §7.2.2, definition of f_p before the citation of Luo–Zhu, p. 71, and the unit property in the first case of the proof, p. 72 (arXiv v5): Defines f_p(n) as the product of the integers 1 ≤ i ≤ n prime to p, equal to n!/(p^{[n/p]}[n/p]!), and uses that f_p(p^α) is a unit of ℤ_p.
- [luo-zhu-2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.02882v1), §3, equation (10), p. 6 (arXiv:2106.02882v1): Defines f_p(n) for every nonnegative integer n by the same product and the same factorial quotient.

<a id="CA-2-p-free-factorial-binomial-factorisation"></a>

#### CA.2.44 Binomial coefficients of multiples of p through the p-free factorial

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/p-free-factorial-binomial-factorisation` · theorem · CA.2 continuation packet

Let p be a prime and f_p the p-free factorial. (a) For n ≥ m ≥ 0: C(np, mp)·f_p(mp)·f_p((n − m)p) = C(n, m)·f_p(np). (b) For n ≥ 1 and m ≥ 0, with generalised binomial coefficients: C(−np, mp)·f_p(mp)·f_p(np) = (−1)^{m(p−1)}·C(−n, m)·f_p(np + mp).

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- p prime; (a) n ≥ m ≥ 0; (b) n ≥ 1, m ≥ 0. The sign (−1)^{m(p−1)} matters only for p = 2.

**Checks.**

- p = 2, n = m = 1: C(−2, 2) = 3 = (−1)¹·C(−1, 1)·f_2(4) = (−1)(−1)·3.
- p = 3, n = 2, m = 1: C(6, 3) = 20 and f_3(6)/(f_3(3)²) = 40/4 = 10 = 20/C(2, 1).
- Checked for p ∈ {2, 3, 5, 7}, n < 9, m < 9.

**Proof sketch.**

1. (a) By the factorial split of p-free-factorial, (kp)! = p^k·k!·f_p(kp) for every k; substitute into C(np, mp) = (np)!/((mp)!((n − m)p)!) and cancel p^n = p^m·p^{n−m}.
2. (b) By Ring.choose_neg, C(−N, M) = (−1)^M·C(N + M − 1, M) for N ≥ 1; and C(N + M − 1, M) = C(N + M, M)·N/(N + M). Apply this to (N, M) = (np, mp) and to (n, m): the ratio C(−np, mp)/C(−n, m) is (−1)^{mp−m}·C((n + m)p, mp)/C(n + m, m), and (a) with (n + m, m) turns this into (−1)^{m(p−1)}·f_p((n + m)p)/(f_p(mp)f_p(np)).

**Needs:** [CA.2/p-free-factorial](#CA-2-p-free-factorial), `mathlib:Ring.choose_neg`, `mathlib:Nat.choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial`, `mathlib:Ring.choose_natCast`.

<a id="CA-2-luo-zhu-congruence"></a>

#### CA.2.45 The Luo–Zhu congruence for p-free factorials

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/luo-zhu-congruence` · theorem · CA.2 continuation packet

Let p be a prime and α ≥ 1 with p odd or α ≥ 2. For every N ≥ 0: f_p(p^α·N) ≡ f_p(p^α)^N (mod p^{2α}). In the excluded case p = 2, α = 1: f_2(2N) ≡ (−1)^{⌊N/2⌋} (mod 4). The exclusion is necessary: f_2(4) = 3 ≢ 1 = f_2(2)² (mod 4).

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- p prime; α ≥ 1; p ≠ 2 or α ≥ 2 for the main congruence; N ∈ ℕ.

**Checks.**

- p = 3, α = 1, N = 2: f_3(6) = 40 ≡ 4 = 2² (mod 9).
- p = 2, α = 2, N = 2: f_2(8) = 105 ≡ 9 = 3² (mod 16).
- Checked for p ∈ {3, 5, 7} with α ≤ 3, p = 2 with α ∈ {2, 3}, and N ≤ 11, and f_2(2N) mod 4 for N < 60; at p = 2, α = 1 the congruence fails exactly for N ≡ 2, 3 (mod 4) in that range.

**Proof sketch.**

1. Induction on N; N = 0 is f_p(0) = 1. For the step, f_p(p^αN) = f_p(p^α(N − 1))·∏\_{1 ≤ i ≤ p^α, p ∤ i}(p^α(N − 1) + i).
2. Modulo p^{2α} the product is f_p(p^α)·(1 + p^α(N − 1)·Σ_{i} i^{−1}), the inverses taken modulo p^{2α} (the cross terms carry p^{2α}).
3. Pair i with p^α − i: 1/i + 1/(p^α − i) = p^α/(i(p^α − i)), so p^α divides the sum of inverses. The pairing has no fixed point because p^{α−1}(p − 1), the number of units, is even and i = p^α/2 is not a unit (p odd, or p = 2 with α ≥ 2); for p = 2, α = 1 the sum is 1 and the argument fails.
4. Hence the factor is ≡ f_p(p^α) (mod p^{2α}) and the induction closes.
5. p = 2, α = 1: f_2(2N) is the product of the odd numbers below 2N, of which ⌊N/2⌋ are ≡ 3 (mod 4).

**Needs:** [CA.2/p-free-factorial](#CA-2-p-free-factorial), `mathlib:Int.ModEq`, `mathlib:ZMod.unitOfCoprime`.

Proposed home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/ClassicalArithmetic/CA2`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

**Sources.**

- [luo-zhu-2019](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.02882v1), §3, Lemma 3.1 with its proof, pp. 6–7 (arXiv:2106.02882v1): States p^{2α} | f_p(p^αn) − f_p(p^α)^n for p odd, α ≥ 1 or p = 2, α ≥ 2, and f_2(2n) ≡ (−1)^{[n/2]} (mod 4); proves the first by expanding the block product modulo p^{2α} and pairing i with p^α − i.
- [yu-2023](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.04659v5), §7.2.2, fact (∗) and the case p = 2, p. 71 (arXiv v5): Quotes the same two congruences as Lemma 3.1 of [LZ16] and uses them in both cases of the proof of Théorème 7.2.3.
- [luo-zhu-2016-preprint](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1611.06506v1), §4, Lemma 4.6 with its proof, pp. 16–17 (arXiv:1611.06506v1): The earlier preprint states the same lemma; its expansion carries a misprint (sourceIssues).

### Digit expansions

p-adic digit expansions and the uniqueness of base-b expansions of real numbers.

<a id="CA-2-p-adic-digit-expansion"></a>

#### CA.2.46 The p-adic digit expansion

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/p-adic-digit-expansion` · construction

For a prime p, every x ∈ ℤ_p has a unique expansion x = ∑\_{i≥0} dᵢpⁱ with digits dᵢ ∈ {0, …, p − 1}; this is an equivalence digitsEquiv : ℤ_p ≃ (ℕ → Fin p), with ∑\_{i&lt;n} dᵢpⁱ = appr x n (Mathlib's `PadicInt.appr`) and dᵢ = ⌊(x mod p^{i+1})/pⁱ⌋. It is a homeomorphism for the product topology on (ℕ → Fin p).

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- p prime (`Fact p.Prime`); digits are the standard representatives 0, …, p − 1.

**API.**

- `PadicInt.digitsEquiv` (equivalence): The equivalence ℤ_p ≃ (ℕ → Fin p), x ↦ its digits.
- `PadicInt.hasSum_digitsEquiv` (characterisation): ∑ dᵢ(x)pⁱ converges to x.
- `PadicInt.sum_digitsEquiv_eq_appr` (compatibility): ∑\_{i&lt;n} dᵢ(x)pⁱ = appr x n (Mathlib's truncation).
- `PadicInt.digitsEquiv_apply` (simp): dᵢ(x) = (toZModPow (i+1) x).val / pⁱ.
- `PadicInt.digitsEquiv_symm_apply` (constructor): digitsEquiv.symm d is the sum ∑ dᵢpⁱ.
- `PadicInt.continuous_digitsEquiv` (structure): digitsEquiv and its inverse are continuous (a homeomorphism with the product topology).

**Unit tests.**

- `PadicInt.digitsEquiv_neg_one` (computation): Every digit of −1 ∈ ℤ_p is p − 1.
- `PadicInt.digitsEquiv_natCast` (compatibility): For n ∈ ℕ, the i-th digit of n ∈ ℤ_p is the i-th entry of Mathlib's `Nat.digits p n` (0 beyond its length).
- `PadicInt.digitsEquiv_zero` (degenerate): All digits of 0 are 0.
- `PadicInt.digitsEquiv_not_additive` (non-example): In ℤ₂, the digit of 1 + 1 at position 1 is 1 while that of 1 is 0: digitsEquiv is not additive.

**Checks.**

- The digits of −1 are all p − 1; the digits of a natural number are its base-p digits followed by zeros.
- Digits are not additive: 1 + 1 = 2 in ℤ₂ has digit 1 in position 1 while 1 has digit 0 there (carries).

**Construction and proof.**

1. Digits: dᵢ(x) = (toZModPow (i+1) x).val / pⁱ; equivalently (appr x (i+1) − appr x i)/pⁱ, which is < p by `PadicInt.appr_lt` and `PadicInt.dvd_appr_sub_appr`.
2. Partial sums: ∑\_{i&lt;n} dᵢpⁱ = appr x n by telescoping, and x − appr x n ∈ pⁿℤ_p (`PadicInt.appr_spec`), so the series converges to x (‖pⁿ‖ → 0, `PadicInt.norm_le_pow_iff_mem_span_pow`).
3. Inverse: for d : ℕ → Fin p the series ∑ dᵢpⁱ converges in the complete ring ℤ_p; its partial sums are its appr, so its digits are d; x is recovered from its digits by `PadicInt.ext_of_toZModPow`.
4. Continuity both ways: the first n digits depend only on x mod pⁿ, and x mod pⁿ only on the first n digits.

**Uses.**

- ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2 (radix expansions): together with Mathlib's Nat.digits and Real.ofDigits it completes the radix expansions of integers, reals and p-adic integers that the stage names
- Milne, ANT, Proposition 7.46: the expansion shows that ℤ_p is compact, the digits giving a finite ε-net at every level
- Keith Conrad, The p-adic expansion of rational numbers: rational numbers are the p-adic numbers with eventually periodic digit expansions

**Needs:** `mathlib:PadicInt`, `mathlib:PadicInt.appr`, `mathlib:PadicInt.appr_spec`, `mathlib:PadicInt.appr_lt`, `mathlib:PadicInt.dvd_appr_sub_appr`, `mathlib:PadicInt.toZModPow`, `mathlib:PadicInt.ext_of_toZModPow`, `mathlib:PadicInt.norm_le_pow_iff_mem_span_pow`, `mathlib:Nat.digits`, `mathlib:ZMod.val`, `mathlib:PadicInt.completeSpace`, `mathlib:NonarchimedeanGroup.multipliable_of_tendsto_cofinite_one`, `mathlib:IsUltrametricDist.nonarchimedeanGroup`.

Proposed home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/Padics/Digits`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic.PadicInt`.

**Sources.**

- [milne-ant-2020](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf), Chapter 7, Proposition 7.26, printed p. 116: The general statement; the node is the case A = ℤ_(p), π = p, S = {0, …, p − 1}, restricted to ℤ_p (no negative powers).
- [milne-ant-2020](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf), Chapter 7, after Proposition 7.26, printed p. 117: The API items `sum_digitsEquiv_eq_appr` and `digitsEquiv_apply`.

<a id="CA-2-canonical-real-expansion-is-recovered"></a>

#### CA.2.47 The canonical base-b expansion is recovered from any expansion not ending in b − 1

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/canonical-real-expansion-is-recovered` · lemma

Let b ≥ 2 and d : ℕ → {0, …, b − 1} with dᵢ ≠ b − 1 for infinitely many i. Then x = ofDigits d = ∑ dᵢ/b^{i+1} lies in [0, 1) and Mathlib's canonical digits of x are d: Real.digits (Real.ofDigits d) b = d.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- b ≥ 2; the digits are indexed so that d₀ is the first digit after the point (Mathlib's `Real.ofDigits`).

**Checks.**

- 0.4999… (b = 10) is excluded: its canonical digits are 0.5000…
- For b = 2 the expansion (1, 0, 1, 0, …) is recovered from its value 2/3.

**Proof sketch.**

1. The tail after position n satisfies 0 ≤ ofDigits (d(· + n)) < 1 strictly, since not all later digits are b − 1 (`Real.ofDigits_const_last_eq_one'` shows that the all-(b − 1) tail has value 1; the converse, that a tail of value 1 has all digits b − 1, is proved by comparing termwise with `Real.ofDigitsTerm_le` and a strict inequality of sums at a digit different from b − 1, `Summable.tsum_lt_tsum_of_nonneg`).
2. Hence ⌊bⁿ⁺¹x⌋ = ∑\_{i≤n} dᵢb^{n−i} (`Real.ofDigits_eq_sum_add_ofDigits`), and Mathlib's digit (Real.digits x b) n = ⌊x·b^{n+1}⌋ mod b is dₙ.
3. In particular x < 1, so x is in the domain [0, 1) of `Real.digits`.

**Needs:** `mathlib:Real.ofDigits`, `mathlib:Real.digits`, `mathlib:Real.ofDigits_eq_sum_add_ofDigits`, `mathlib:Real.ofDigits_const_last_eq_one'`, `mathlib:Real.ofDigits_digits`, `mathlib:Real.ofDigitsTerm_le`, `mathlib:Summable.tsum_lt_tsum_of_nonneg`.

<a id="CA-2-uniqueness-of-base-b-expansions"></a>

#### CA.2.48 Uniqueness of base-b expansions of real numbers

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/uniqueness-of-base-b-expansions` · theorem

Let b ≥ 2 and d, e : ℕ → {0, …, b − 1}. Then ∑ dᵢ/b^{i+1} = ∑ eᵢ/b^{i+1} iff d = e, or, after possibly swapping d and e, there is n with dᵢ = eᵢ for i < n, dₙ = eₙ + 1, dᵢ = 0 and eᵢ = b − 1 for i > n. In particular every x ∈ [0, 1) has exactly one expansion not ending in b − 1, and exactly two expansions iff x is a nonzero b-adic fraction k/bᵐ.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- b ≥ 2; values in [0, 1]; the value 1 has the single expansion (b − 1, b − 1, …).

**Checks.**

- 0.1 = 0.0111… in base 2 (n = 0); 1/2 = 0.5 = 0.4999… in base 10.
- x = 1/3 has the unique binary expansion 0.0101…

**Proof sketch.**

1. If d ≠ e let n be the first index where they differ, say dₙ > eₙ. Cancelling the common prefix and multiplying by b^{n+1}, (dₙ − eₙ) + tail(d) = tail(e) with tails in [0, 1] (`Real.ofDigits_eq_sum_add_ofDigits`).
2. Since tail(e) ≤ 1 and dₙ − eₙ ≥ 1, equality forces dₙ − eₙ = 1, tail(d) = 0 (all later dᵢ = 0) and tail(e) = 1; that tail(e) = 1 forces all later eᵢ = b − 1 is the converse of `Real.ofDigits_const_last_eq_one'`, proved by termwise comparison with `Real.ofDigitsTerm_le` and `Summable.tsum_lt_tsum_of_nonneg`.
3. The converse is the geometric series identity (b − 1)∑\_{i>n} b^{−i−1} = b^{−n−1}.
4. The consequence follows with canonical-real-expansion-is-recovered.

**Needs:** [CA.2/canonical-real-expansion-is-recovered](#CA-2-canonical-real-expansion-is-recovered), `mathlib:Real.ofDigits`, `mathlib:Real.ofDigits_eq_sum_add_ofDigits`, `mathlib:Real.ofDigits_const_last_eq_one'`, `mathlib:Real.ofDigits_SurjOn`, `mathlib:Real.ofDigitsTerm_le`, `mathlib:Summable.tsum_lt_tsum_of_nonneg`.

Proposed home: `TauCeti/Analysis/Real/Digits`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic.Real`.

**Sources.**

- [planetmath-decimalexpansion-2013](https://planetmath.org/existenceanduniquenessofdecimalexpansion), Section 2.2, Near-uniqueness for non-negative numbers: The theorem; the node makes the exceptional pair explicit.

<a id="CA-2-automata-with-output"></a>

#### CA.2.49 Deterministic finite automata with output

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/automata-with-output` · definition

A deterministic automaton with output (DFAO) with input alphabet α, states σ and output alphabet Δ is a transition function δ : σ → α → σ, an initial state q₀ ∈ σ and an output function τ : σ → Δ. It runs on a word (a list) from the head of the list: evalFrom s [a₁, …, a_m] = δ(…δ(δ(s, a₁), a₂)…, a_m), and eval = evalFrom q₀. Finiteness of σ is imposed where it is used. For S ⊆ Δ, the acceptor toDFA S is Mathlib's `DFA` with the same transitions and accepting states τ⁻¹(S).

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- No finiteness in the structure (as Mathlib's `DFA`); `IsAutomatic` requires a Fintype of states.
- Words are read from the head of the list, as `DFA.eval` (List.foldl).

**API.**

- `DFAO` (structure): A DFAO: step : σ → α → σ, start : σ, output : σ → Δ.
- `DFAO.evalFrom` (data): Run from a state on a word, head first.
- `DFAO.eval` (data): Run from the initial state.
- `DFAO.evalFrom_append` (simp): evalFrom s (x ++ y) = evalFrom (evalFrom s x) y.
- `DFAO.toDFA` (compatibility): The acceptor DFA with accepting states output⁻¹(S).
- `DFAO.eval_toDFA` (compatibility): (toDFA S).eval = eval.
- `DFAO.mem_accepts_toDFA` (characterisation): x ∈ (toDFA S).accepts iff output (eval x) ∈ S.
- `DFAO.mapOutput` (functoriality): Change the output alphabet along f : Δ → Δ'.
- `DFAO.prod` (constructor): The product automaton, with output pairs.
- `DFAO.evalFrom_nil` (simp): Running from a state s on the empty word returns s.
- `DFAO.evalFrom_cons` (simp): Running from s on a :: x is running from step s a on x.
- `DFAO.eval_mapOutput` (simp): Changing the output map by f does not change the state reached: (mapOutput f).eval = eval, so the output becomes f ∘ output.
- `DFAO.eval_prod` (simp): The product automaton reaches the pair of the states the two factors reach: (prod M N).eval w = (M.eval w, N.eval w).

**Unit tests.**

- `DFAO.parity_eval` (computation): The automaton on Fin 2 with states ZMod 2, step s a = s + a, start 0 and identity output returns the parity of the number of ones of the word.
- `DFAO.eval_nil` (degenerate): eval [] = start.
- `DFAO.toDFA_accepts` (compatibility): The acceptor for S = univ accepts every word (agreement with Mathlib's DFA.accepts).

**Checks.**

- The two-state parity automaton outputs the parity of the number of ones.
- On the empty word the output is τ(q₀).

**Construction and proof.**

1. Define the structure with fields step, start, output; define evalFrom by List.foldl and eval.
2. evalFrom (x ++ y) = evalFrom (evalFrom x) y by List.foldl_append (as `DFA.evalFrom_of_append`).
3. toDFA S: the DFA ⟨step, start, output⁻¹' S⟩; its eval agrees with the DFAO's, so its language is {w | τ(eval w) ∈ S} (`DFA.mem_accepts`).
4. Constructions: mapOutput f post-composes τ with f; prod runs two automata in parallel with pair output.

**Uses.**

- [CA.2/automatic-sequences](#CA-2-automatic-sequences): k-automatic sequences are those computed by a DFAO with finitely many states on base-k digits
- [CA.2/automatic-iff-finite-kernel](#CA-2-automatic-iff-finite-kernel): the kernel automaton has the kernel as its state set
- Bridy, Section 2.2: p-representations and their DFAOs give the complexity bounds of Christol's theorem

**Needs:** `mathlib:DFA`, `mathlib:DFA.eval`, `mathlib:DFA.evalFrom`, `mathlib:DFA.evalFrom_of_append`, `mathlib:DFA.accepts`, `mathlib:DFA.mem_accepts`.

Proposed home: `TauCeti/Computability/DFAO`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic.DFAO`.

**Sources.**

- [bridy-automaticcurves-2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.08241v2), Section 2.1, p. 3: The structure. Bridy takes the input alphabet, the output alphabet and the states finite; here the structure assumes none of these, IsAutomatic adds a Fintype of states and fixes the finite input alphabet Fin k, and the output alphabet stays arbitrary (only the range of the output map is finite).
- [christol-suitesalgebriques-1980](http://www.numdam.org/item/10.24033/bsmf.1926.pdf), Section 4, p. 405: The same data (states Σ, output alphabet Ξ, input alphabet [k] = {0, …, k − 1}).

**First-pass review finding.** DFAO,evalFrom,eval,toDFA,mapOutput,prod are six data declarations bundled into one node. Split data declarations and consumed append API per lemma-level rule.

<a id="CA-2-dfao-output-reversal"></a>

#### CA.2.50 Reversing all words of a finite output automaton

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/dfao-output-reversal` · lemma

For any input alphabet α, finite state type σ, output alphabet Δ and DFAO M on α with states σ, there is a DFAO N with finitely many states such that N.output(N.eval(w)) = M.output(M.eval(reverse(w))) for every word w. This includes empty words and arbitrary zero padding, without a canonical-digit restriction.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- No finiteness assumption on α or Δ; finiteness of σ suffices.

**Unit tests.**

- `reversal_order` (computation): For the automaton on ZMod 3 with initial state 0, transition q↦q+1 on false and q↦2q on true, the words [false,true] and [true,false] reach 2 and 1 respectively.

**Checks.**

- The empty word returns the original initial output.
- A noncommuting transition pair is composed in reverse order; a parity-only test would not detect an incorrect order.
- The equality holds on padded words, not only canonical expansions.

**Proof sketch.**

1. Let E be the finite image of M.output. Use the finite set of functions σ → E as states, with initial function q ↦ M.output(q), transition g on a given by q ↦ g(M.step(q,a)), and output g(M.start).
2. Induction on w gives the stronger state identity g_w(q) = M.output(M.evalFrom(q,reverse(w))). Evaluate at M.start.
3. Encode the finite state set by Fin of its cardinality when the target existential requires states in Type; this avoids imposing a universe restriction on Δ.

**Needs:** [CA.2/automata-with-output](#CA-2-automata-with-output), `mathlib:Fintype.equivFin`.

Lean names: `DFAO.exists_output_reverse`. Proposed home: `TauCeti/Computability/Automatic/Cobham`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

**Sources.**

- [krebs-cobham-2018](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1801.06704v1), Definition 2 and Lemma 5, p.1; direct reversal construction extending the inherited reading-direction proof: The source uses finite output automata on all words. This is the explicit worker deduction needed to preserve that convention under reversal.

<a id="CA-2-automatic-sequences"></a>

#### CA.2.51 k-automatic sequences

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/automatic-sequences` · definition

Let k ≥ 1 (NeZero k). A sequence a : ℕ → Δ is k-automatic if there are a finite type σ and a DFAO M with input alphabet Fin k and states σ such that a(n) = τ(eval((n)\_k)) for every n, where (n)\_k = Nat.digits k n is the base-k expansion of n read least significant digit first (Mathlib's order; (0)\_k is empty), mapped into Fin k.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- Reading convention: least significant digit first ('lecture inverse' of Christol–Kamae–Mendès France–Rauzy, 'reverse reading' of Bridy); for k ≥ 2 the other convention gives the same class (automaticity-is-independent-of-reading-direction); for k = 1 the unary digit word is its own reversal.
- Canonical representations, without padding zeros, as Mathlib's `Nat.digits`; states live in Type (as Mathlib's `Language.IsRegular`).
- The output alphabet Δ is arbitrary; automaticity forces the range of a to be finite.
- Base k = 1 extends the sources: Bridy (p. 3), Christol–Kamae–Mendès France–Rauzy (p. 405) and Byszewski–Konieczny (p. 6) all take k ≥ 2. With NeZero k, base 1 reads the unary word Nat.digits_one; only the constructors (constants, eventually periodic sequences) are claimed for it, and every theorem in this layer assumes k ≥ 2.

**API.**

- `IsAutomatic` (data): a is k-automatic (least significant digit first, canonical digits).
- `IsAutomatic.map` (functoriality): If a is k-automatic so is f ∘ a.
- `IsAutomatic.prod` (constructor): If a and b are k-automatic so is n ↦ (a n, b n).
- `IsAutomatic.finite_range` (other): A k-automatic sequence takes finitely many values.
- `isAutomatic_const` (constructor): Constant sequences are k-automatic.
- `isAutomatic_of_eventually_periodic` (constructor): Eventually periodic sequences are k-automatic for every k.

**Unit tests.**

- `isAutomatic_const_two` (degenerate): A constant sequence is 2-automatic.
- `not_isAutomatic_id` (non-example): n ↦ n (with values in ℕ) is not 2-automatic: it takes infinitely many values.
- `isAutomatic_parity` (computation): n ↦ n mod 2 is 2-automatic (the output reads the first digit read, the last digit of n).
- `isAutomatic_unary_mod_three` (degenerate): The sequence n -> n mod 3 is 1-automatic: Nat.digits_one encodes a unary word, and a three-state cycle counts its length modulo 3.

**Checks.**

- n ↦ n mod 2 is 2-automatic, n ↦ n is not automatic in any base (infinite range).
- The Thue–Morse sequence is 2-automatic with two states.

**Construction and proof.**

1. Define IsAutomatic k a := ∃ (σ : Type) (\_ : Fintype σ) (M : DFAO (Fin k) σ Δ), ∀ n, a n = M.output (M.eval ((Nat.digits k n).map (Fin.ofNat k))).
2. Closure: mapOutput gives IsAutomatic.map; the product automaton gives IsAutomatic.prod; the range is contained in the finite image of the output function.
3. Constant sequences use one state. For an eventually periodic sequence with preperiod N and positive period p, construct the automaton directly, without using the later finite-kernel theorem. When k >= 2 its finite state stores the accumulated value truncated at N, that value modulo p, the place value truncated at N, and the place value modulo p. On a digit d, add d times the place value and multiply the place value by k. Output a at the accumulated value when it is below N, otherwise at the unique representative in [N,N+p) of its residue modulo p. Induction on the least-significant-first digits proves correctness. When k = 1, Nat.digits_one gives n identical letters after mapping to Fin 1; use N+p states that count to N and then cycle with period p. This covers the unary case separately.

**Uses.**

- [CA.2/christol-theorem](#CA-2-christol-theorem): the coefficient sequences of algebraic series over 𝔽_q are exactly the p-automatic ones
- [CA.2/thue-morse-sequence](#CA-2-thue-morse-sequence): the Thue–Morse sequence is the model 2-automatic sequence
- DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.5/mahler-values-transcendence-dichotomy: for automatic series and rational α the dichotomy is Cobham's conjecture (its acceptance), so automatic generating series are the model Mahler functions
- Christol–Kamae–Mendès France–Rauzy, Section 8: with Cobham's theorem: a sequence both k- and k′-automatic for multiplicatively independent k, k′ is eventually periodic

<a id="CA-2-k-kernel"></a>

#### CA.2.52 The k-kernel of a sequence

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/k-kernel` · definition

The k-kernel of a : ℕ → Δ is the set of subsequences n ↦ a(k^e n + r) with e ≥ 0 and 0 ≤ r < k^e.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- k ≥ 2 for the theorems; the definition makes sense for every k.

**API.**

- `kernel` (data): The set {n ↦ a(k^e n + r) | e ≥ 0, r < k^e}.
- `self_mem_kernel` (simp): a ∈ kernel k a.
- `kernel_subset` (other): If b ∈ kernel k a then kernel k b ⊆ kernel k a.

**Unit tests.**

- `kernel_const` (degenerate): The 3-kernel of a constant sequence is the singleton of that sequence.
- `kernel_parity` (computation): The 2-kernel of n ↦ n mod 2 is {n ↦ n mod 2, the constant 0, the constant 1}.
- `kernel_thueMorse_eq_pair` (computation): The 2-kernel of the Thue–Morse sequence is {t, n ↦ 1 + t n} (in ZMod 2).
- `kernel_two_mul_add_one_mem` (characterisation): n ↦ a(2n + 1) belongs to the 2-kernel of a (e = 1, r = 1), while r ≥ k^e is not allowed.

**Checks.**

- The kernel of a constant sequence is a singleton; the 2-kernel of the Thue–Morse sequence is {t, 1 − t}.
- Finiteness of the kernel is the automaticity criterion (next node).

**Construction and proof.**

1. Define kernel k a as a set of sequences.
2. a ∈ kernel k a (e = 0, r = 0); the kernel of a kernel element is contained in the kernel (k^e(k^{e′}n + r′) + r = k^{e+e′}n + (k^e r′ + r)).

**Uses.**

- [CA.2/automatic-iff-finite-kernel](#CA-2-automatic-iff-finite-kernel): Eilenberg's criterion
- [CA.2/cartier-operators](#CA-2-cartier-operators): the kernel of the coefficient sequence of f is the orbit of f under the Cartier operators
- [CA.2/thue-morse-sequence](#CA-2-thue-morse-sequence): the Thue–Morse kernel has two elements

**Needs:** `mathlib:Set.Finite`.

<a id="CA-2-automatic-iff-finite-kernel"></a>

#### CA.2.53 Eilenberg's theorem: automatic iff finite kernel

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/automatic-iff-finite-kernel` · theorem

Let k ≥ 2 and a : ℕ → Δ. Then a is k-automatic iff its k-kernel is finite. Moreover a DFAO whose states are the kernel elements computes a, reading least significant digit first, and it gives the same output on every base-k representation of n with trailing (leading-zero) padding.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- k ≥ 2; no finiteness assumption on Δ.

**Checks.**

- The Thue–Morse kernel has 2 elements and the kernel automaton is the two-state parity automaton.
- n ↦ n has an infinite kernel (the sequences n ↦ k^e n + r are pairwise distinct).

**Proof sketch.**

1. (⇒) Let M generate a with states σ. For n ≥ 1 the digits of k^e n + r are the e digits of r padded with zeros followed by the digits of n (`Nat.digits_append_zeroes_append_digits` with e − |(r)\_k| zeros, which is at least 0 because r < k^e by `Nat.digits_length_le_iff`), so a(k^e n + r) = τ(evalFrom (q_{e,r}) ((n)\_k)) with q_{e,r} = eval (padded r); for n = 0 it is a(r). Hence the kernel element (e, r) is determined by the pair (q_{e,r}, a(r)) ∈ σ × range(τ), a finite set.
2. (⇐) Take as states the finite kernel, initial state a, output b ↦ b(0), and transition b ↦ (n ↦ b(kn + d)) on digit d; this stays in the kernel (kernel_subset). Induction on the digits shows that after reading (n)\_k from state b the state is m ↦ b(k^{len} m + n), whose value at 0 is b(n); with b = a this is a(n). Appending zero digits does not change the output, which gives the padding statement.

**Needs:** [CA.2/automatic-sequences](#CA-2-automatic-sequences), [CA.2/k-kernel](#CA-2-k-kernel), [CA.2/automata-with-output](#CA-2-automata-with-output), `mathlib:Nat.digits_append_digits`, `mathlib:Nat.digits_add_two_add_one`, `mathlib:Set.Finite`, `mathlib:Nat.digits_append_zeroes_append_digits`, `mathlib:Nat.digits_length_le_iff`.

The explicit kernel transitions b ↦ (n ↦ b(kn + d)) are the node's own.

<a id="CA-2-automaticity-is-independent-of-reading-direction"></a>

#### CA.2.54 Automaticity does not depend on the reading direction

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/automaticity-is-independent-of-reading-direction` · theorem

Let k ≥ 2 and a : ℕ → Δ. Then a is k-automatic (least significant digit first) iff some DFAO with finitely many states computes a(n) by reading the base-k digits of n most significant digit first.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- Canonical digits (no leading zeros) in both conventions.

**Checks.**

- The two-state Thue–Morse automaton works in both directions (its transitions commute).
- The state count can grow: reversal may need up to |range τ|^{|σ|} states (Bridy, Remark 2.5 for acceptors: 2ⁿ).

**Proof sketch.**

1. Given M = (σ, δ, q₀, τ) reading least significant digit first, build M′ with states the functions σ → Δ, initial state τ, transition f ↦ (q ↦ f(δ(q, d))) and output f ↦ f(q₀). By induction, after reading the reversed word w^R the state is q ↦ τ(evalFrom q w), so the output on (n)\_k reversed is τ(eval (n)\_k) = a(n). The state set Δ^σ may be restricted to the finite set of reachable functions (their values lie in range τ, finite).
2. The converse is the same construction applied to the reversed word.

**Needs:** [CA.2/automatic-sequences](#CA-2-automatic-sequences), [CA.2/automata-with-output](#CA-2-automata-with-output).

<a id="CA-2-automatic-in-base-a-power"></a>

#### CA.2.55 k-automatic iff k^m-automatic

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/automatic-in-base-a-power` · theorem

Let k ≥ 2 and m ≥ 1. A sequence is k^m-automatic iff it is k-automatic.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- k ≥ 2, m ≥ 1.

**Checks.**

- The Thue–Morse sequence is 4-automatic (and 2^m-automatic for every m).
- It is not 3-automatic (Cobham's theorem, which this node does not use).

**Proof sketch.**

1. By Eilenberg's theorem it suffices to compare kernels. The k^m-kernel is contained in the k-kernel (exponent me).
2. Conversely, write a k-kernel element with exponent e = mq + j (0 ≤ j < m) and r = r₀ + k^{mq}r₁ with r₀ < k^{mq}, r₁ < k^j: then k^e n + r = k^{mq}(k^j n + r₁) + r₀, so it is n ↦ b(k^j n + r₁) with b = (n ↦ a(k^{mq}n + r₀)) in the k^m-kernel; finitely many b, j < m and r₁ < k^j give finitely many elements.

**Needs:** [CA.2/automatic-iff-finite-kernel](#CA-2-automatic-iff-finite-kernel), [CA.2/k-kernel](#CA-2-k-kernel), [CA.2/automatic-sequences](#CA-2-automatic-sequences).

<a id="CA-2-automatic-iff-uniform-morphism"></a>

#### CA.2.56 Cobham's characterisation by uniform morphisms

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/automatic-iff-uniform-morphism` · theorem

Let k ≥ 2. A sequence a : ℕ → Δ is k-automatic iff there are a finite alphabet Γ, a k-uniform morphism φ : Γ → Γ^k, a letter-to-letter coding τ : Γ → Δ and a fixed point s of φ (s(kn + r) = φ(s(n))\_r for all n and r < k, in particular φ(s(0))₀ = s(0)) with a = τ ∘ s.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- k ≥ 2; the fixed point is encoded by the equations s(kn + r) = φ(s n) r, which determine s from s(0).

**Checks.**

- Thue–Morse: Γ = {0, 1}, φ(0) = 01, φ(1) = 10, τ = id, s = 0110 1001 ….
- The Baum–Sweet sequence: Γ = {a, b, c, d}, φ(a) = ab, φ(b) = cb, φ(c) = bd, φ(d) = dd, τ(a) = τ(b) = 1, τ(c) = τ(d) = 0 (Christol–Kamae–Mendès France–Rauzy, p. 404).

**Proof sketch.**

1. (⇐) Read the digits of n most significant first: s(n) = δ\*(s(0), (n)\_k^R) for the automaton with transitions δ(x, r) = φ(x)\_r, since s(kn + r) = φ(s n)\_r; leading zeros are harmless because φ(s(0))₀ = s(0). Output τ; conclude by automaticity-is-independent-of-reading-direction.
2. (⇒) Take a most-significant-first automaton (σ, δ, q₀, τ) with δ(q₀, 0) = q₀: the reversal (automaticity-is-independent-of-reading-direction) of the kernel automaton of automatic-iff-finite-kernel has this property, because its initial state is the output map b ↦ b(0) and b(k·0) = b(0). Put Γ = σ, φ(q)\_r = δ(q, r) and s(n) = δ\*(q₀, (n)\_k reversed); then s(kn + r) = φ(s n)\_r and a = τ ∘ s.

**Needs:** [CA.2/automatic-sequences](#CA-2-automatic-sequences), [CA.2/automaticity-is-independent-of-reading-direction](#CA-2-automaticity-is-independent-of-reading-direction), [CA.2/automatic-iff-finite-kernel](#CA-2-automatic-iff-finite-kernel).

- [christol-suitesalgebriques-1980](http://www.numdam.org/item/10.24033/bsmf.1926.pdf), Section 3, p. 404: The fixed point of a k-uniform morphism, encoded in the node by s(kn + r) = φ(s n)\_r.

<a id="CA-2-eventually-periodic-sequences-are-automatic"></a>

#### CA.2.57 Every eventually periodic sequence is automatic

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/eventually-periodic-sequences-are-automatic` · lemma

For any k≥1, a sequence f:ℕ→Δ satisfying f(t+p)=f(t) for all t≥N, with p≥1, is k-automatic in the existing canonical-digit convention. This promotes the existing automatic-sequences API item to a prerequisite node; it introduces no second declaration.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- Base 1 uses Mathlib’s unary digit-list convention and is treated separately.
- No finiteness assumption on Δ is needed.

**Unit tests.**

- `finite_prefix` (non-example): The sequence with value 7 at zero and n mod 2 at positive n has period 2 on n≥1 but its values at 0 and 2 differ.
- `unary_eventually_periodic` (compatibility): The sequence with value 7 at zero and n mod 2 at positive n is 1-automatic in the existing unary convention.

**Checks.**

- A special initial value followed by a periodic tail is allowed.
- Base 1 is not covered by the kernel criterion and is handled by its unary counter.
- For N=0,p=1 the counter is the one-state constant automaton.

**Proof sketch.**

1. The sequence is determined by its first N+p values, so its range is finite.
2. For k ≥ 2 use the direct automaton of automatic-sequences. Its finite state holds the value read so far and the current place value k^L, each cut off at N and also reduced modulo p. A digit d adds d times the place value and multiplies the place value by k; both updates are computable from the stored data. The output is f at the value if it is below N, and otherwise f at the representative in [N, N+p) of its residue. Induction on the least-significant-first digits proves correctness without the finite-kernel theorem, so the declaration stays before Eilenberg's theorem.
3. For k=1, Nat.digits 1 t has length t. Mapping into Fin 1 makes every input digit zero. A finite counter with states 0,…,N+p−1 advances through the prefix then cycles through N,…,N+p−1, outputting the corresponding value of f. It computes the unary word of length t exactly.

**Needs:** [CA.2/automatic-sequences](#CA-2-automatic-sequences), [CA.2/automata-with-output](#CA-2-automata-with-output), `mathlib:Nat.digits_one`.

Lean names: `isAutomatic_of_eventually_periodic`. Proposed home: `TauCeti/Computability/Automatic/Basic`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

<a id="CA-2-thue-morse-sequence"></a>

#### CA.2.58 The Thue–Morse sequence

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/thue-morse-sequence` · definition

The Thue–Morse sequence t : ℕ → 𝔽₂ is t(n) = s₂(n) mod 2, the parity of the sum of the binary digits of n: 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, …. It satisfies t(2n) = t(n) and t(2n + 1) = 1 + t(n), is 2-automatic with 2-kernel {t, 1 + t}, is the fixed point of 0 ↦ 01, 1 ↦ 10, and its generating series T = ∑ t(n)Xⁿ ∈ 𝔽₂⟦X⟧ satisfies (1 + X)³T² + (1 + X)²T + X = 0.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- Values in ZMod 2 = 𝔽₂, so that 1 − t = 1 + t and the algebraic equation is over 𝔽₂.

**API.**

- `thueMorse` (data): t(n) = s₂(n) mod 2 ∈ ZMod 2.
- `thueMorse_two_mul` (simp): t(2n) = t(n).
- `thueMorse_two_mul_add_one` (simp): t(2n + 1) = 1 + t(n).
- `isAutomatic_thueMorse` (example): t is 2-automatic.
- `kernel_thueMorse` (characterisation): The 2-kernel of t is {t, 1 + t}.
- `thueMorse_algebraic` (relation): (1 + X)³T² + (1 + X)²T + X = 0 in 𝔽₂⟦X⟧ for T = ∑ t(n)Xⁿ.

**Unit tests.**

- `thueMorse_values` (computation): t(0), …, t(7) = 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1.
- `thueMorse_two_pow` (computation): t(2^j) = 1 for every j.
- `thueMorse_not_eventually_periodic` (non-example): t is not eventually periodic, so its series is not rational (a periodic mis-definition fails this).

**Checks.**

- t is not eventually periodic, so T is algebraic of degree 2 but not rational.
- t(2^j) = 1.

**Construction and proof.**

1. Define t n := (Nat.digits 2 n).sum cast to ZMod 2.
2. t(2n) = t(n), t(2n + 1) = 1 + t(n) from Nat.digits 2 (2n + r) = r :: Nat.digits 2 n for n ≥ 1 (`Nat.digits_add_two_add_one`).
3. Kernel: by the two relations, n ↦ t(2^e n + r) is t or 1 + t according to the parity of s₂(r); both occur. Automaticity: the two-state parity automaton, or Eilenberg's theorem.
4. Algebraic equation: splitting n by parity, T = ∑ t(n)X^{2n} + X∑(1 + t(n))X^{2n} = (1 + X)T(X²) + X/(1 + X)² over 𝔽₂ (1 − X² = (1 + X)²), and T(X²) = T² (Frobenius on 𝔽₂⟦X⟧); multiplying by (1 + X)² gives (1 + X)³T² + (1 + X)²T + X = 0 (Christol–Kamae–Mendès France–Rauzy p. 403).
5. Nonperiodicity test: if an eventual period p is even, restrict t(2n)=t(n) to halve p until it is odd, p=2q+1. The two parity identities and periodicity give t(n)=1+t(n+q) and t(n+q+1)=1+t(n) for large n. Applying the first identity to n+1 then gives t(n+1)=t(n). This eventual constancy contradicts t(2^j)=1 and t(3\*2^j)=0 for arbitrarily large j. Rational generating series over a finite field imply an eventual recurrence, whose finite windows force eventual periodicity; hence the nonrationality test follows.

**Uses.**

- [CA.2/christol-theorem](#CA-2-christol-theorem): the Thue–Morse series is the standard algebraic, non-rational example
- Christol–Kamae–Mendès France–Rauzy, Section 8: the transcendence of ∑ t(n)2^{−n} (Dekking, Kubota, Loxton–van der Poorten) motivates Cobham's conjecture
- DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.5: Mahler functions: T(z) satisfies a Mahler equation in z ↦ z²

**Needs:** [CA.2/automatic-sequences](#CA-2-automatic-sequences), [CA.2/k-kernel](#CA-2-k-kernel), `mathlib:Nat.digits`, `mathlib:Nat.digits_add_two_add_one`, `mathlib:PowerSeries.mk`, `mathlib:ZMod`.

Proposed home: `TauCeti/Computability/Automatic/ThueMorse`, `TauCeti.ClassicalArithmetic`.

**Sources.**

- [byszewski-konieczny-automatic-2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08979), Section 1, p. 6 and p. 8: The API items `thueMorse_two_mul`, `thueMorse_two_mul_add_one` and `kernel_thueMorse`; the definition is on p. 6 ('t_n = 1 if s₂(n) is odd and t_n = 0 if s₂(n) is even').
- [christol-suitesalgebriques-1980](http://www.numdam.org/item/10.24033/bsmf.1926.pdf), Section 2, pp. 402 to 403: The API item `thueMorse_algebraic` (p. 403), the model instance of Christol's theorem; p. 402 also records that a sequence is eventually periodic exactly when its series is rational (algebraic of degree 1), which is the step from the nonperiodicity test to nonrationality.

### Christol's theorem

Cartier operators on Laurent series over 𝔽_q, Ore relations, and the equivalence of algebraicity and q-automaticity.

<a id="CA-2-cartier-operators"></a>

#### CA.2.59 The Cartier operators on Laurent series

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/cartier-operators` · definition

For a field K, positive modulus q and r ∈ ℕ, the Cartier operator on K⸨X⸩ is Λ_r(∑ aₙXⁿ) = ∑ a_{qn+r}Xⁿ. It is K-linear. When r < q it preserves power series and polynomials, with degree at most natDegree P / q on a polynomial P. For finite K with q = |K| it satisfies Λ_r(gᵠh) = g·Λ_r(h), and f = ∑\_{r&lt;q} X^r(Λ_r f)^q. Define the unused q = 0 value to be zero; the coefficient specification applies only for q > 0.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- q > 0 is necessary for bounded-below Laurent support; r < q is necessary for the power-series and polynomial preservation statements.
- The Frobenius identities require finite K and q = |K|, so c^q = c for c ∈ K.
- The value at q = 0 is an explicitly specified junk value, not a coefficient-decimation operator.

**API.**

- `LaurentSeries.cartier` (data): For q > 0, coefficient decimation Λ_r on Laurent series; cartier 0 r f = 0 by convention.
- `LaurentSeries.cartier_zero` (simp): cartier 0 r f = 0 (the explicit junk-value convention).
- `LaurentSeries.coeff_cartier` (simp): For q > 0: (Λ_r f).coeff n = f.coeff (q\*n+r), for every n ∈ ℤ.
- `LaurentSeries.cartier_add` (simp): Λ_r(f + g) = Λ_r f + Λ_r g.
- `LaurentSeries.cartier_smul` (simp): Λ_r(c f) = c Λ_r f for c ∈ K.
- `LaurentSeries.cartier_ofPowerSeries` (compatibility): For q > 0 and r < q, Λ_r of ∑ aₙXⁿ is the power series ∑ a(qn+r)Xⁿ.
- `LaurentSeries.cartier_pow_card_mul` (relation): For |K| = q: Λ_r(gᵠh) = g·Λ_r h.
- `LaurentSeries.eq_sum_single_mul_cartier_pow` (relation): For |K| = q: f = ∑\_{r&lt;q} X^r (Λ_r f)^q.
- `LaurentSeries.natDegree_cartier_le` (other): For q > 0 and r < q, Λ_r of P is a polynomial P′ with natDegree P′ ≤ natDegree P / q.

**Unit tests.**

- `LaurentSeries.cartier_single` (computation): Λ_r(X^m) = X^{(m−r)/q} if q ∣ m − r, and 0 otherwise (0 ≤ r < q).
- `LaurentSeries.cartier_one_zero` (degenerate): With modulus 1, Λ₀ is the identity.
- `LaurentSeries.cartier_pow_card` (characterisation): Over a finite field with q elements, Λ₀(gᵠ) = g.
- `LaurentSeries.cartier_zero_modulus` (degenerate): cartier 0 0 1 = 0. The coefficient formula cannot hold at q = 0, because it would give nonzero coefficients at every negative exponent.
- `LaurentSeries.cartier_outside_residue_range` (non-example): cartier 1 1 1 = X⁻¹: without r < q, a power series can decimate to a Laurent series with a negative exponent.

**Checks.**

- Λ_r(X^m) = X^{(m−r)/q} if m ≡ r (mod q) and 0 otherwise.
- With q = 1, Λ₀ is the identity.
- Over a finite field, Λ₀(gᵠ) = g.
- q = 0 is excluded from coefficient decimation: for f = 1, r = 0 the proposed coefficient function is 1 at every exponent and has no lower support bound.
- Power-series preservation requires r < q; cartier 1 1 1 = X⁻¹ is a counterexample without that hypothesis.

**Construction and proof.**

1. For q > 0 the coefficient function n ↦ f.coeff (q\*n+r) has bounded-below support because multiplication by positive q is order preserving on ℤ. Set cartier 0 r f = 0 separately.
2. Linearity is coefficientwise (and trivial at q = 0). For q > 0 and r < q, a negative n has q\*n+r < 0; thus decimation of a power series has no negative coefficients and agrees with the decimated sequence under HahnSeries.ofPowerSeries.
3. For |K| = q: (∑ bₙXⁿ)^q = ∑ bₙ^q X^{qn} = ∑ bₙX^{qn} (Frobenius and `FiniteField.pow_card`), so the coefficient of X^{qn+r} in gᵠh is ∑\_m b_m h_{q(n−m)+r}, which is the coefficient of Xⁿ in g·Λ_r(h).
4. f = ∑\_r X^r(Λ_r f)^q by splitting exponents by residue mod q and the same Frobenius computation.
5. For q > 0 and r < q, decimation of P is a polynomial: its negative coefficients vanish and its nonzero exponents satisfy q\*n+r ≤ natDegree P, giving natDegree Λ_r(P) ≤ natDegree P / q.

**Uses.**

- [CA.2/algebraic-series-are-automatic](#CA-2-algebraic-series-are-automatic): the finite set H of Christol–Kamae–Mendès France–Rauzy §7 is stable under the Λ_r
- [CA.2/automatic-series-are-algebraic](#CA-2-automatic-series-are-algebraic): f = ∑ X^r(Λ_r f)^q expresses each kernel series through q-th powers
- Bridy, Section 3: the twisted Cartier operators on differentials of a curve bound the automaton size

<a id="CA-2-ore-relation"></a>

#### CA.2.60 Ore relations for algebraic power series over a finite field

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/ore-relation` · lemma

Let K be a finite field with q elements and f ∈ K⟦X⟧ algebraic over K[X] (equivalently over K(X)). Then there are m ≥ 0 and a₀, …, a_m ∈ K[X] with a₀ ≠ 0 such that ∑\_{i=0}^m aᵢ f^{qⁱ} = 0.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- Algebraic is Mathlib's `IsAlgebraic K[X] f` for the K[X]-algebra K⟦X⟧ (`PowerSeries.algebraPolynomial`).

**Checks.**

- For rational f = P/Q ≠ 0: P^{q−1}Q·f − Q^q·f^q = 0 is an Ore relation with a₀ = P^{q−1}Q ≠ 0.
- Thue–Morse (q = 2): subtracting the square of (1 + X)³T² + (1 + X)²T + X = 0 from X times it removes the constant term and gives X(1 + X)²T + (1 + X)³T² + (1 + X)⁶T⁴ = 0, an Ore relation with a₀ = X(1 + X)² ≠ 0.
- The relation cannot in general be taken with a₀(0) ≠ 0 (above, a₀(0) = 0), which is why the proof divides by a₀ in K⸨X⸩ rather than in K⟦X⟧.

**Proof sketch.**

1. The K(X)-span of f, f^q, f^{q²}, … lies in the finite extension K(X)(f) ⊆ K⸨X⸩, so for m = [K(X)(f) : K(X)] these m + 1 elements are linearly dependent; clearing denominators gives a nontrivial relation ∑ aᵢf^{qⁱ} = 0 with aᵢ ∈ K[X].
2. Among all nontrivial relations choose one whose least index j with a_j ≠ 0 is minimal, and suppose j ≥ 1. Since a_j = ∑\_r X^r(Λ_r a_j)^q, some Λ_r(a_j) ≠ 0.
3. Apply Λ_r: as f^{qⁱ} = (f^{q^{i−1}})^q, Λ_r(aᵢf^{qⁱ}) = Λ_r(aᵢ)f^{q^{i−1}} (cartier-operators), giving a relation ∑\_{i≥j} Λ_r(aᵢ) f^{q^{i−1}} = 0 whose least index is j − 1 with nonzero coefficient, a contradiction; so j = 0.

**Needs:** [CA.2/cartier-operators](#CA-2-cartier-operators), `mathlib:IsAlgebraic`, `mathlib:PowerSeries.algebraPolynomial`, `mathlib:FiniteField.pow_card`, `mathlib:RatFunc.coeToLaurentSeries`, `mathlib:IsFractionRing.isAlgebraic_iff`, `mathlib:IntermediateField.adjoin.finiteDimensional`.

<a id="CA-2-algebraic-series-are-automatic"></a>

#### CA.2.61 Algebraic power series over 𝔽_q have q-automatic coefficients

`ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2/algebraic-series-are-automatic` · theorem

Let K be a finite field with q elements and f = ∑ aₙXⁿ ∈ K⟦X⟧ algebraic over K[X]. Then (aₙ) is q-automatic.

**Hypotheses and conventions.**

- K finite, q = |K|.

**Checks.**

- Thue–Morse: the relation (1 + X)³T² + (1 + X)²T + X = 0 yields a finite Λ-stable set; the kernel has 2 elements.
- Rational series (degree 1) give eventually periodic, in particular automatic, sequences.

**Proof sketch.**

1. By ore-relation, ∑\_{i=0}^k aᵢf^{qⁱ} = 0 with a₀ ≠ 0. Put g = f/a₀ ∈ K⸨X⸩; then g = ∑\_{i=1}^k bᵢ g^{qⁱ} with bᵢ = −aᵢa₀^{qⁱ−2} ∈ K[X].
2. Let N = max(deg a₀, deg bᵢ) and H = {∑\_{i=0}^k cᵢg^{qⁱ} : cᵢ ∈ K[X], deg cᵢ ≤ N}, a finite set (K finite). f = a₀g ∈ H.
3. H is stable under every Λ_r: for h = ∑ cᵢg^{qⁱ}, substituting g = ∑ bᵢg^{qⁱ} in the i = 0 term gives h = ∑\_{i≥1}(c₀bᵢ + cᵢ)g^{qⁱ}, so Λ_r(h) = ∑\_{i≥1} Λ_r(c₀bᵢ + cᵢ)g^{q^{i−1}} (cartier-operators), with deg Λ_r(c₀bᵢ + cᵢ) ≤ 2N/q ≤ N.
4. Hence the Λ-orbit of f, which is the set of generating series of the q-kernel of (aₙ) (`LaurentSeries.cartier_ofPowerSeries`), is finite; by automatic-iff-finite-kernel, (aₙ) is q-automatic.

**Needs:** [CA.2/ore-relation](#CA-2-ore-relation), [CA.2/cartier-operators](#CA-2-cartier-operators), [CA.2/k-kernel](#CA-2-k-kernel), [CA.2/automatic-iff-finite-kernel](#CA-2-automatic-iff-finite-kernel), [CA.2/automatic-sequences](#CA-2-automatic-sequences), `mathlib:FiniteField.pow_card`.
